summary: Mark Tatz (1946–2021) was a scholar of Buddhist studies and Tibetology. He earned his PhD from the University of British Columbia under Leon Hurvitz in 1978 and was attested as a professor at the California Institute of Integral Studies in 1988.

Mark Teeuwen (b. 1966) specializes in Japanology and religious studies. He completed his MA and PhD at Leiden University, lectured at Cardiff University (1994–1999), and was appointed professor at the University of Oslo in 1999.

Mark Unno works in Buddhist studies, religious studies, and Japanology. Educated at Oberlin College (~1977–1981) and Stanford University (~1987–1994), he has held posts at Brown University and the University of Oregon (assistant professor around 2000).

Markus Gabriel (b. 1980) is a philosopher who studied at the University of Bonn (~2002–2005). He held posts at Bonn (~2009), UC Berkeley (~2012–2013), and The New School (~2014–2015), becoming Global Senior Advisor at the Kyoto Institute of Philosophy in 2024.

Markus Viehbeck is a scholar of Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He earned his PhD in 2012 at the University of Vienna under Helmut Tauscher and Franz-Karl Ehrhard, later working as a Heidelberg University project researcher and Vienna faculty member (attested 2026).

Marsha Weidner works in Sinology, art history, and Buddhist studies. She earned her PhD from the University of California, Berkeley, and held posts as assistant professor at the University of Virginia (attested 1990) and professor at the University of Kansas (attested 2001).

Marshall Sahlins (1930–2021) was an anthropologist and historian. He studied at the University of Michigan (~1947–1952) and Columbia University (~1952–1954), later holding faculty appointments at the University of Michigan (~1957–1973) and the University of Chicago (appointed 1973).

Marta Sernesi is a scholar of Tibetology and Buddhist studies. She earned her PhD from the University of Turin in 2007 and was attested as a visiting professor at the Göttingen Academy of Sciences and Humanities in 2026.

Martha Ann Selby (b. 1954) is an Indologist. Attested in 2026, she is professor emeritus at the University of Texas at Austin and serves at Harvard University as Sangam Professor of South Asian Studies, Comparative Literature professor, and department chair.

Martha C. Nussbaum (b. 1947) is a philosopher educated at NYU and Harvard, where she studied under Bernard Williams. Her career includes faculty posts at Harvard, Brown, and the University of Chicago, where she became a distinguished service professor in 1995.

Martin Baumann (b. 1960) works in religious and Buddhist studies. He completed a PhD at Leibniz University Hannover (~1990–1993) and a Habilitation at Leipzig University (~1994–1999) before becoming professor of religious studies at the University of Lucerne in 2001.

Martin Brauen (b. 1948) specializes in Tibetology, art history, and Buddhist studies. Educated at Delhi and Zurich (doctoral degree), he served as curator and department head at the University of Zurich's Ethnographic Museum (from 1975) and chief curator at the Rubin Museum (2008–2012).

Martin Collcutt (b. 1939) is a scholar of Japanology, history, and Buddhist studies. Educated at Cambridge and Harvard (PhD 1975), he taught at Yokohama National and Tokyo universities before serving as professor and East Asian Studies director at Princeton (1975–2015).

Martin Delhey specializes in Indology and Buddhist studies. He completed his PhD at the University of Hamburg in 2002 under Lambert Schmithausen, later holding posts at Hamburg, Göttingen, Ryukoku, Shandong, and the International Institute for Buddhist Studies (attested 2026).

Martin Haug (1827–1876) was an Indologist and linguist who studied under Rudolf von Roth and Theodor Benfey. He held posts at Deccan College (1859–1866) and the University of Munich, where he was appointed professor of Sanskrit and comparative philology in 1868.

Martin Heidegger (1889–1976) was a German philosopher. He studied under Heinrich Rickert at the University of Freiburg, where he completed his studies in 1916 and later taught (1915–1923, 1936–1940), alongside a professorship at the University of Marburg (1923–1928).

Martin Joachim Kümmel (b. 1970) is a linguist and Indologist. He earned his master's, doctorate, and Habilitation at the University of Freiburg, where he was an assistant and academic councillor (~1999–2007) before taking a chair at the University of Jena in 2013.

Martin King Whyte (b. 1942) is a sociologist of China. Educated at Cornell and Harvard (PhD 1971), he held faculty appointments at the University of Michigan (1970–1994), George Washington University (1994–2000), and Harvard University (from 2000).

Martin Lehnert is a scholar of Sinology, Buddhist studies, and religious studies. He earned his PhD from the University of Freiburg and was attested in 2016 as Professor of East Asian Religion and Philosophy at the University of Munich.

Martin Lowenthal works in Buddhist and religious studies. He studied under traditional teachers Tenzin Wangyal Rinpoche and Namkhai Norbu, and he has held posts at Boston College and Harvard University.
